reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A potentially life-threatening autoimmune blistering disease that most often begins with painful, non-healing oral erosions before skin involvement appears
Blisters are flaccid and fragile because the split is within the epidermis, so intact bullae are rarely seen and the picture is dominated by raw erosions
Gentle lateral pressure on skin can extend a blister or shear the epidermis (positive Nikolsky sign), reflecting loss of keratinocyte adhesion
Any patient with persistent unexplained mucosal erosions, particularly in the mouth, should raise suspicion for pemphigus
Diagnosis rests on skin biopsy showing suprabasal acantholysis and direct immunofluorescence demonstrating intercellular IgG deposition in a fishnet pattern
Circulating antibodies to desmoglein 3 (with or without desmoglein 1) can be detected serologically and correlate with disease activity
Management relies on systemic immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunomodulators or B-cell-depleting therapy for extensive disease
Meticulous wound care, pain control, nutritional support, and vigilance for infection are essential given widespread skin barrier loss
reference.pathophysiology: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease in which IgG autoantibodies target desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease), transmembrane desmosomal cadherins that mediate keratinocyte adhesion. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal function and triggers intracellular signalling that causes loss of cell-to-cell adhesion (acantholysis). This produces a suprabasal split within the epidermis, giving rise to fragile flaccid blisters and erosions. Because desmoglein 3 is expressed strongly in mucosa, mucosal disease often predominates; involvement of both desmogleins produces combined mucosal and cutaneous lesions. Extensive erosions lead to fluid loss, protein depletion, and susceptibility to secondary infection and sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous pemphigoid (tense blisters, subepidermal split, older patients)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Aphthous stomatitis or herpetic gingivostomatitis for oral-only disease
additionalInvestigations: Skin or mucosal biopsy for histology showing suprabasal acantholysis
Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence showing intercellular IgG and C3
Serum indirect immunofluorescence and desmoglein antibody assays to support diagnosis and monitor activity
Screening for underlying malignancy if paraneoplastic pemphigus is suspected
Baseline and monitoring investigations before and during immunosuppressive therapy, including infection screening
redFlags: Extensive skin and mucosal erosion with fluid and protein loss and risk of sepsis
Inability to eat or drink due to painful oropharyngeal involvement
Signs of secondary bacterial infection or systemic instability
Features suggesting paraneoplastic pemphigus, which mandates malignancy evaluation
reference.prognosis: Once frequently fatal, pemphigus vulgaris now has a much better outlook with immunosuppressive and B-cell-depleting therapy; however, it remains a serious chronic disease and much of the residual mortality relates to treatment complications and infection.
pitfalls: Dismissing chronic oral erosions and delaying diagnosis until skin disease is widespread
Confusing it with bullous pemphigoid and misjudging severity and treatment intensity
Under-appreciating infection risk from extensive barrier loss and immunosuppression
Tapering immunosuppression too rapidly and precipitating relapse
management: Induce remission with systemic corticosteroids combined with rituximab as first-line therapy
Use adjuvant immunosuppression such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil to spare corticosteroids
Provide intravenous immunoglobulin or immunoadsorption for severe or refractory disease
Give supportive wound care with fluid and protein replacement for extensive erosions and treat secondary infection
Provide analgesia, oral care and a soft diet for painful oral erosions to maintain nutrition
Monitor disease activity with anti-desmoglein-3 and anti-desmoglein-1 titres and screen for treatment-related infection and bone loss
Exclude an underlying malignancy where paraneoplastic pemphigus is suspected
Escalate to inpatient specialist care for widespread erosions with fluid loss and sepsis risk
